These two questions refer to matters of internal management in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, having to do with salaries of major and minor employees. It has always been the practice in the house to decline to bring down details of this kind in connection with the Canadian National Railways, and I think that a similar policy should be adopted with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I realize that these questions can be presented to a special committee in the case of the Canadian National Railways, and in my opinion the government must consider whether a special committee of the house should not review the position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That can be taken up another year.

From the date of the establishment of the radio commission until last year this house insisted upon having presented to it every detail with reference to the persons who occupied positions in that commission-what salaries they received and the dates of their appointment, and many other questions as well. I regard it as wholly erroneous and at variance with the general principle that governs the Canadian National matter to say that that rule should apply in this connection. The house has a right to all the information it is possible to receive with respect to the radio commission, which stands on a basis entirely different from that of the Canadian National Railways. I protest against this question not being answered; I protest against the attitude taken by the government in connection with it. It is at variance with their own established policy during five years. One recalls by looking at Hansard the attacks that were made upon the commission and the salaries paid, and to say that this house should not have that information now is to say that when in opposition we can insist on receiving information which under different circumstances we decline to give to the house. I think that on reconsideration the minister will conclude that the house has a right to the information. If he lets the question stand it would perhaps serve the immediate purpose.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is the trade agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom, signed at Ottawa on February 23, 1937:
The governments of Canada and of the United Kingdom, recognizing that the revival and development of trade is an essential feature of the prosperity and well-being of all countries and to this end desiring further to facilitate trade and commerce between Canada and the United Kingdom, and having resolved to replace by the present agreement the agreement concluded between them at Ottawa on the 20th August, 1932, have agreed upon the following provisions:
Article 1:	The government of the United
Kingdom undertake that goods grown, produced or manufactured in Canada and consigned from any part of the British Empire which are now free of duty, shall continue to enjoy entry free of customs duty into the United Kingdom, subject, however to the reservations set forth in schedule I appended hereto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to read schedule I.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Schedule I is as follows:
As regards eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products, the government of the United Kingdom reserve to themselves the right, if they consider it necessary in the inter-iwts of the United Kingdom producer to do to review at any time the basis of preference so far as relates to the articles above enumerated and after notifying the Canadian government either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce whilst maintaining preferential margins, or in consultation with the Canadian government to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market.
IMr. Bennett.]

Mr. Chairman, the items mentioned in the schedule may be dealt with by the United Kingdom in a manner different from that in which they are now dealt with. I take that to be the sense of it. The old agreement contained a provision whereby, by mutual consent, there could be a modification of the agreement then made. This schedule provides that if there is a duty imposed by the United Kingdom they will consult with us and that we may .have a preference; is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; schedule I compares with schedule A of the former agreement, and refers to certain dairy products. The provisions of schedule I are similar to the provisions of the old schedule A, with the difference of course that the three years certain mentioned in schedule A expired two years ago. Since that time the United Kingdom have had the right to do what schedule A empowered them to do, but they have not yet done so. They continue to reserve the right to do so.

I suppose the minister
does not place upon schedule I the construction the present Prime Minister placed upon it in 1932-that this is an intimation that England proposes to do it. I placed upon Hansard the observations in that regard made by the right hon. gentleman. He said it was quite clear that that was what England proposed to do. Has the minister any reason for believing that Great Britain has any greater intention to do it now than she had formerly? Has the government any reason to believe that the United Kingdom does contemplate taking such action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The position in that regard, Mr. Chairman, is not dissimilar from what it was in 1932, in that the United Kingdom then and since was engaged in a highly technical inquiry into industries covered by these commodities. At the time of the negotiations last summer the inquiry had not been concluded. Certain advances had been made, but the United Kingdom desired to be left as free in the new agreement as in the old one. I believe I am correct in saying that the report on one phase of the matter has been presented-the British milk report is now down, and of course it is available to the British government for consideration in formulating its own policy. It was with respect to that report particularly, and detailed examinations which were taking place with respect to other phases of the industry, that the British government desired under the new agreement to reserve its freedom of action, in the same degree as they had possessed it under the old one, after the expiry of the first three years.

Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement

Yes; in other words, there were (three years in which we had the preference, that is, to 1935. The five years do not expire until 1937, but on August 20, 1935, the three years expired. After that Great Britain had freedom of action with respect to eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and milk products. But that freedom of action was limited to (a) imposition of a duty with a preference in favour of Canada, or (b) regulation by quota of importations from this country; or possibly both. The investigations ito which the minister has referred were concluded, I believe, some time ago. I believe they were completed before we left office, as a matter of fact, but the report was not made. The investigations with respect to some matters have been completed for some time. The question of a report is another matter altogether. This we regarded, and do regard, as a matter of very great importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

If Great Britain is to regulate by quota the extent to which we may export eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and milk products to that country, then of course it becomes important, from our standpoint, lest the quota limited to Canada be such as to make our further operations very much restricted. That is one point we had under consideration.
The question of duties was very strong in the mind of one member of the British government. And the agricultural population of Great Britain, as indicated by the farmers' organization, is strongly in favour of a tariff against colonial and dominions produce. Of course this would probably apply equally to New Zealand or Australia. If it were applied to Canada it might become of transcendant importance. I do not know ito what extent the minister is able to give further information about it, but certainly in the fall of 1935, at the time the late government left office, the end of .the three years had almost been reached. Since that time the government of Great Britain has been carrying forward these investigations, looking towards the inauguration of a new policy. Whether or not that policy will come into being-of course it is entirely speculation on my part- I am asking the minister if he has any reason to believe that we might contemplate the imposition of a duty on Canadian eggs, butter, cheese or other milk products or, in the second place, the restriction of the extent of our exports by quantitative regulations in the form of quotas, or a combination of both. That is the only point to which I wish to direct attention; perhaps the minister can enlighten us upon it.
Do the numbers of these items correspond with the numbers of the items in the agreement passed at the session of 1930? If not, would it be possible to have such a list?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member will notice in the Votes and Proceedings of February 25 that there is a column containing figures in black type; then another column shows the existing rates which are the rates of the 1932 agreement between Canada and Great Britain. I understand the comparison my hon. friend wants to make is with a prior period?
With 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no agreement in 1930. I did not think of bringing down comparative material of that type; it would have represented a considerable amount of work. I suggest to my hon. friend that he can obtain that information by having before him the Hansard of 1930 giving the budget. That would be a simple way of doing it. Any information I could furnish would simply be a reproduction, of the Hansard of that date. It is a little difficult to answer the leader of the opposition as one cannot know the mind of the British government with respect to the report which is before it.
I only wanted to know what had been expressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are certain things that may be gathered from the report itself. The recommendation, now under consideration by the British government does not deal with import duties; it is a rather non-committal report in that regard,. It emphasizes the domestic market situation rather than import control. It cannot be said to be conclusive with respect to either of the alternatives contemplated in schedule I of this agreement or in schedule A of the old agreement. I notice my right hon. friend emphasized, and quite properly, the fact that the word "or" is used in schedule I, as it was used in schedule A of the old agreement. That is to say, the qualification involves either a preferential duty on Canadian produce, or, in consultation with the Canadian government, the bringing of such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market. That appears in schedule I, but it may not be adopted by the British government. I cannot say to my right hon. friend that I have any information that the British government is intending to adopt either alternative.

That is all I want to know.

There is a distinction
without a difference.

I fancy that very few hon. members have had an opportunity to read the report of the import duties advisory committee of July 1935, and it might be desirable, inasmuch as we are perpetuating these arrangements, that such a statement be given by the minister so that it might appear on the record and references be made to it at any time.

speechtext: Anticipating that difficulty, Mr. Chairman, the nature of which my right hon. friend is aware-

speechtext: -I draw attention to the fact that in appendix B, on page 40 of the copy of the trade agreement and connected papers, will be found the proposals for the modification of the import duty on lead and the provisions of the Ottawa agreements relating thereto, under which we are at present operating. For reasons which they state to be connected with defence, there is a strong desire on the part of the British government to build up a zinc and lead industry in England itself. That is, indeed, part of the reason for the annex to which I have just made reference, and is further clarified by reading letter No. 1 on page 38 of the document now before members of the committee, which is a letter on this matter from the Prime Minister of Canada to Sir Francis Floud, High Commissioner in Canada for the United Kingdom. Letter No. 1
Ottawa, February 23, 1937.
Sir,
With reference to article 16 of the trade agreement signed this day, I have the honour to inform you that the Canadian government, having taken note of the statements of the United Kingdom government in the course of the recent discussions:
(1)	that it is essential to the national security that the production of the zinc smelting industry in the United Kingdom should be maintained at a satisfactory level;
(2)	that at any enquiry into the question of the effects of imports of zinc from oversea empire countries on the maintenance of the production of zinc in the United Kingdom at a satisfactory level having regard to the needs of national security, the Canadian zinc producers would have the opportunity of submitting evidence, and
(3)	that the government of the United Kingdom would consult the Canadian government before taking any decision to impose a customs duty on imports of Canadian zinc into the United Kingdom,
agree that it will be open to the United Kingdom government, after such enquiry and after consultation with the Canadian government, and notwithstanding the provisions of article 1 of the trade agreement, to impose a customs duty on imports of zinc produced or manufactured in Canada, without prejudice however, to the provisions of article 3 of the agreement.

The maintenance of the preference.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,

-agree that it will be open to the United Kingdom government, after such inquiry and after consultation with the Canadian government. and notwithstanding the provisions of article 1 of the trade agreement, to impose a customs duty on imports of zinc produced or manufactured in Canada, without prejudice however, to the provisions of article 3 of the agreement.

What it was desired to do was what the minister said, namely, to make it without prejudice to the maintenance of the preference; but what is contained in this document is without prejudice to the provisions of article 3.

I congratulate them
upon the maintenance of the industry in the old country and I hope that this government will follow that principle and not be so hard on the industry in Canada.

Hear, hear.

This gentleman said: "The only thing I can say is we have lost part of our market, but we are nearer to England than you are, and we perhaps study their requirements a little more closely than you do."

As sure as we are here, Mr. Chairman, this idea of using the British market as a convenience and using the United States as the market that serves you, is entirely wrong. When you find some difficulty, because of tariffs or otherwise, you turn to the British market, but you give them no constancy or

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is our difficulty.

Of course it is; as I pointed out last year, I felt that when we negotiated the agreement with the United States. You see, if we could look to the United States with the same degree of certainty as we can look to Great Britain in connection with the marketing situation it would be entirely different, but we do not know what sudden changes may take place in the attitude of the legislators to the south of us, whereas with respect to our own country wTe have every assurance that nothing will be done that will be prejudicial to the interests of the dominions or their market in Great Britain without complete discussion and timely notice. I can only say that I look upon the addition of beef and cattle to this agreement as representing the effort the English consumer has made to ensure some steadiness of supply from this country, but it does appear to be fairly clear that as things now are the number of cattle that will go from Canada to Great Britain will not be very great. As a matter of fact our cattle exports have been getting smaller, as compared with .the days when we had to deal with the problem of the relaxation of regulations and restrictions that tied us u>p. I was looking up the figures not long since. I wonder how many members of this house realize that at one time we shipped over 200,000 head of cattle to Great Britain in one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We shipped 216,000 head in 1927.
If you go back to the eighties, when we were relatively a poor country-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am wrong; the figure I gave was the total exports.
I thought it was rather prior to that.

In 1922 we sold over 200000 head to Great Britain. That trade was carried on in the old days until some low tariff -man such as President Cleveland of the United States would come into power and say, "I guess we will let Canadian cattle in." Then for three or four years Canadian cattle would be sent to that market, and the British market would be lost. Then President Wilson came along and we got free entry. After that everything went south; then one morning we found ourselves without a market at all, and people were ruined. Those familiar with ranching in western Canada know that some

of the largest ranchers went bankrupt. One gentleman, whose assets at one time were estimated at $7,000,000, did not leave an estate large enough on his death to pay the costs of probate, and that was brought about by the emergency United States tariff on our cattle.
If the government can do anything to assure a steady supply of cattle to the British market, I think it should be done. I know how difficult it is, because certainly I have tried. We should not allow the idea to develop that the only market for Canadian beef and cattle is the market to the south. If we could induce our people to ship a steady flow of even 50,000 head of cattle per annum it would mean a great deal, so long as 50,000 head went forward each year. But when you have 50,000 one year, 25,000 another year and 75,000 another year, with uncertainty as to the flow of cattle across the ocean, you will have just the condition that confronted us. I have no hope, for instance, that under changed conditions we shall continue to have ready access to the United States market. That may continue to be the case during the term of the Democratic party, but you must look a good deal further ahead than that. It is not a matter of five or six or eight or ten years; you must take the long view of it.
I am sorry to see this item extended to include beef and cattle, but on the other hand I quite appreciate the reason for it, and since it is here I think we must do our very best to assist the British government. But I am quite sure that if conditions were reversed the welkin would ring in this parliament, as it rang in 1932. We would be told that to take our policy from the United Kingdom or to undertake to assist Great Britain to carry into effect its policy, which is its business, would be so very contrary to the whole spirit of our institutions that I would almost expect them to fall.

I think the remarks of the leader of the opposition are very timely. Only the other day I noticed in the Commercial Intelligence Journal that we were not keeping up a constant supply of live stock for the old country market, which made it difficult to secure the confidence of those engaged in that trade there. Speaking from memory I believe that last year we exported to the United Kingdom about 33,000 head of cattle, though we had the privilege of shipping at least 50,000 head to that market. This year I believe the number is even smaller, due to the fact that prices have been much better in the United States. You cannot blame the breeders of cattle for selling in the best market, and that is why cattle are going to

the United States at the present time. I do believe, however, that it is very important that we should strive to maintain our market in the old country, which after all is the most stable of all export markets. I think the government might very well undertake some scheme under which a fund would be created-
Subsidies.

Pay a subsidy, if you wish, so that a situation such as exists to-day might be looked after, and so that we might guarantee to the old country market at least 10,000 head of cattle per month the year round. Then, when the price dropped in the old country, or when the price in the United States or any other market exceeded the price in the old country and the Canadian producer desired to get all he could out of his cattle, the government could step in and subsidize the breeder of cattle so that at least those 10,000 head per month would go forward to the old country market. I think that suggestion is worthy of consideration. I believe it will have to be done unless we are prepared to reestablish that market every few years, which is very hard to do. We should endeavour to maintain that market, and it seems to me something could be done in the way of undertaking to furnish a continuous supply of cattle to the old country.

I think the suggestion that has been advanced by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) is an excellent one. Really I cannot see how we can maintain a steady flow of bacon without some such scheme. I was wondering whether the leader of the opposition would tell us what ideas he had in mind for stabilizing the market. If there is something better than a subsidy, we are ready to listen to it.

Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, and the desirability of maintaining a supply of beef cattle in the British market, may I say that I entirely agree with the desirability of achieving that end. In the past, one of the great difficulties has been the securing of shipping equipped to carry cattle. A shipping concern wishing to carry cattle must maintain stalls on its ships, and the equipment for handling cattle, and by installing that equipment they find it difficult fully to utilize their space on return cargoes. For this reason shipping companies have been somewhat loath to fit out their ships, because the original cost runs about $14 to $16 per stall. They do not wish to make this expenditure unless they are assured of a continuous supply of cattle.
That is one factor, a very important one, with which we have had difficulty in the past. I agree that we have used the British cattle 31111-112
market as a convenient market or, perhaps I should say, a convenience market-a market to suit our convenience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is better.

When we have a surplus we supply it, but when the United States market opens up and other conditions are advantageous, we desert the market in the old country. That is a bad state of affairs, and one which I believe could be overcome by organization among the larger shippers, who export cattle in substantial quantities, of which there are only about half a dozen. So far as the number engaged is concerned, the matter could be handled easily. I believe there could be cooperation among the larger shippers, and shipping companies, and perhaps the government would sit in. The question of subsidy might arise, but I believe the problem could be overcome without going that far. When subsidies are paid a condition is immediately created which very often in the long run will do more harm than good. I believe the matter could be dealt with without resorting to subsidies.
I rose to speak particularly with regard to the British bacon market, which is of vastly more importance to the Canadian producer than is the cattle market. One of our difficulties in the British market lies in the fact that Canada has not made a genuine effort to put on that market the best bacons she can produce. I am not making that statement carelessly, because I hold in my hand the sworn statement of Mr. E. J. Smith, the president of the packers' association, who at the time in question admitted that grade A bacon, which fixes the price of Canadian bacon on the British market-and incidentally, on the sworn evidence of Mr. Stanley McLean, fixes the price of hogs in Canada-consisted of sides varying in weight from 50 to 70 pounds. They are grouped 50 to 55 pounds, 55 to 60 pounds, 60 to 65 pounds and 65 to 70 pounds, and all go into grade A. He further admitted, according to his evidence which I have under my hand, that the hogs which went into the production of those sides included selects, bacon, lights and heavies. Any farmer who sells hogs knows that when he sells a heavy or a light he is penalized a dollar' or a dollar and a half, and sometimes as much as two dollars for that hog, as against the base price which is based upon bacon hogs.
Someone may say, " Well, the difficulty is to get selects and bacons." Again I refer to the sworn evidence of Mr. Stanley McLean, in which he admitted that fifty per cent of the hogs would grade selects or bacons. If our export business were composed more largely of selects and bacons the Canadian farmer would be getting a better price in Canada for his hogs. Even with the tremendous in-

Has my hon. friend allowed for the time factor? I was told in Great Britain that that is important.
Mr. STEVE,NS: In order to adjust the time factor all that one has to do is to compare the Canadian hog price with the bacon price of two months away. It will be seen upon examining the statement that there is little difference. There is such a uniformity in the prices for hogs that the variations in the prices of bacon are not reflected properly, apart altogether from the comparison with Dutch prices. All one has ,to do is to adjust the time between the purchase of the hogs and the production of the bacon, which is well determined. There is no difficulty in doing that.
Why is it that the Danes get from 10 to 14 shillings, and not very long ago as high as 19 shillings, above ,t'he Canadian price? We know that Canadian bacon made from select and bacon grade hogs is on a parity with the best Danish bacon. The chef at the Picadilly hotel at London made a test of Russian bacon, Canadian bacon, Danish bacon and another type. This gentleman is one of the most noted chefs in London and without knowing the origin of the different bacons he was testing, he gave first place to the Canadian. This bacon was produced by Schneider's of Kitchener, a very good company but shipping only comparatively small quantities. There is a point I should like to draw to the attention of the government at this time, one which is vital to this transaction we have made with Great Britain. We have the bacon hog grades of lights, heavies, bacons and selects, and then we have four definite grades of bacon ranging from 50-55, 55-60, 60-65 and 65-70. Why is that done? I will tell you. This matter was brought to my attention some years ago when I was Minister of Trade and Commerce. I had a conference with the representatives of the Canadian packers and against my wishes they gained their argument that there was a market for number two bacon in England. Therefore, they insisted on this 31111-1121
differentiation in the classes of hogs. No man can say that a heavy hog will produce as good bacon as a select or bacon type hog, especially for a discriminating market such as Great Britain. They insisted upon this variation in the grading of hogs.
This brings us to another point. How is the price of bacon fixed in England, or in the London market? The price of Canadian bacon is fixed by a committee composed exclusively of Britishers, representatives of British importers and distributors. I do not for a moment suggest that they are not fine people and good businessmen; I think it will be found that they are among the best. But I submit that it is absolutely unfair, bearing in mind that the price of British bacon fixes the price not only of the hogs that aTe shipped overseas but of the sixty or seventy per cent that are not so shipped, to have the price of Canadian bacon determined by a committee composed entirely of representatives of distributing houses in England. I know it will be answered that some of these gentlemen represent the Canadian distributors. That is true:	Canada
Packers have as their agents some of these gentlemen who are in business over there, making their profit out of the bacon they sell in England, and I certainly should expect them to look after their own interests first. The packers are protected, because, on their own statements, according to a letter written by Mr. McLean in January of this year, they know what to expect on the British market; they know how that market declines in certain months in the autumn, and they anticipate that decline; and the price of hogs in Toronto, in Winnipeg and in other Canadian markets drops in anticipation of the decline they anticipate, based upon their knowledge over a period of years of the British market.
My reasons for saying what I have said are these. First, I want to emphasize the value of the British market to the Canadian producer, but I lay upon this government the responsibility of seeing that the producer gets the full value of that market. That, I think, is a duty which rests upon us as a parliament, and particularly upon the government. I believe that, as the price spreads report recommends, we should inquire carefully as to this committee which fixes the price of Canadian bacon in the British market; we should ascertain definitely whether the Canadian farmer is getting a return equal to that of his competitors in other countries.
There is no differential in the practice of packing. We can cure and pack these products just as cheaply as any country in the

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member leaves the subject of bacon and hogs, would he mind indicating what steps he thinks should be taken to confine the grade within the limits to which in his opinion it should be confined?

Yes. I am not pitting my judgment against that of others; I am basing my statement on the views of experts; and I have no hesitation in saying that the weights fifty-five to fifty and fifty-five to sixty, which is the way they are now graded, should be included-but none others-in grade A.

And only from
selects.

And they should be from selects and bacons. I should like to say a word or two about grading. We have a very good grading system, particularly where hogs are sold on open markets, but great numbers of hogs are delivered direct to the packing plants. The system may have been changed in the last year or two-if it has I do not know_but formerly they were not graded or weighed under government supervision when they were delivered direct; and we recommended definitely, and I have an idea that the recommendation was adopted, that they should be weighed by government weighers when delivered direct to the packers. I would put only these two particular grades under grade A, and I would classify the others as grade B. and let grade B have the lower price. If we did that, grade A would be well up to the Danish price, and what a difference it would make to the Canadian producer, even on the present allocation of price in Canada by the packers, if instead of getting 79 shillings he got 89 or 92 shillings, which would be ten or twelve shillings more for the higher grade. So long as you have in grade A heavies and lights and other classes which have no business there at all, the whole grade gets a lower price than Danish bacon; whereas if the selects and the bacons only were included in the grade A class you would get ten to twelve shillings, and in some cases

more than that, above the present price, which would be reflected in the return to the producers.
I intend to conclude with a word on this particular clause. On the face of things it might look as though we were blindly complying with an agreement to restrict, or permitting one party to the bargain to impose arbitrary restrictions. But that is not at all the point at issue; it never has been. The point at issue is that, due to propinquity and its standard of quality, Danish bacon secured a very strong hold on the British market, as also did the bacon of Poland, Ireland, Holland and some other countries. They were improving their standard of products, were in close touch with the British market, and gave good service. By reason of distance we were at a considerable disadvantage. But in 1932 the British, very generously, I think, with respect to an item of this kind, because as the Minister of Finance knows, from time immemorial bacon has been looked upon as a favourite item almost a sacred, on the British breakfast table-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Particularly bacon.

Particularly bacon. Great
Britain gave us a quota of two and a half million hundredweight on the British market, which was far beyond anything that we were then equipped to supply; in fact, up to the present we have supplied, I think, not more than half that quantity in any one year. In doing that the British government had to impose a quota on other countries, that is, notify other countries that they could not exceed a certain amount. If we had suddenly increased our production without notice to them, and without any assurance that it would be maintained, it would have disturbed their whole internal market as well as their relations with other countries. Therefore they asked that Canada advise them from time to time what she could supply; I believe the request was that we should indicate for three month periods, as long as six months ahead, what the probable supply would be.

That is the present
arrangement.

It is simply a common
sense, businesslike request from the British government to ourselves, and everything possible should be done as no doubt is being done, to comply with it.
The fixing of the price of Canadian hogs by the price of bacon in Great Britain lays upon the government as well as upon those who control the packing business a most onerous responsibility. Personally I do not

Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement
believe that the Canadian hogs slaughtered and marketed- as Canadian bacon should necessarily be on the same basis as export bacon. I know that the general law applies; but after all, in these days the general laws of supply and demand and so forth are being shot to pieces, to use a colloquialism, by every country in the world, and we are faced with these conditions everywhere. My opinion is that we should study these matters first from the standpoint of the producer, because if there is one class that has suffered it has been the producer, particularly producers of live stock and wheat.
I have one further observation to make; I do not like to say this, but perhaps it ought to be said. The argument is advanced that if you look at the profit on meats you will find that it is only a quarter of a cent per pound, or something like that; and of course, if you accept that at its face value, you are silenced; there is no answer. But this is what I cannot get over. During the last six years Canadian farmers as a class from- coast to coast have been suffering perhaps mo-re than any other class because of the low prices of cattle and hogs. The Canadian farmer has been suffering hardships which he ought not to be asked to bear. But during these same years the packing industry has passed through the most prosperous period in its existence. It will be observed that in a four year period- it may have been a five year period prior to 1935-they set aside, in addition to these depreciation reserves to which I have referred, reserves equal to one-half their total capital and had further reserves that were not disclosed until uncovered by an- investigation. Again, I am not for a moment saying that merely for the purpose of calling attention to this healthy condition shall I say among the packers; but I do say that in the light of all the other points I have raised it is due to the farmer that this house should scrutinize, and scrutinize with a degree of attention approaching suspicion-, some of the statements that are made to farmers as an excuse for the low price of their products.

I appreciate the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens). The difference between what the Dutch farmer gets for his bacon and the price in England, and the difference between what the Canadian farmer gets and the price of Canadian bacon in Britain, is a question that should be very seriously considered by this house. Unquestionably the Canadian packers are making it difficult for the Canadian farmer to raise pigs. I am sure that those who have raised pigs in Canada must realize that they have been doing so at a loss for a number of years. I
have here a letter from Mr. Stanley McLean of Canada Packers, an outstanding man, who disagrees with some of the opinions that have been expressed. He says:
In other words, if Canadian hogs had been as good as Danish hogs, the Canadian farmer in the last three years would have received for the hogs he produced an additional $12,000,000 per year.
That is an important statement.
The fact that the Canadian, farmer did not receive this extra $12,000,000 per year was a misfortune.
That is from Mr. Stanley McLean of Canada Packers. It is believed that the spread is too great between the price paid in Great Britain and the price paid here to the Caaadian farmer. The hon. member has referred to the differential in prices, and I was going to bring that up. I have figures-they are the same as he has given

showing an average of about 4-7 cents as the differential between what the Canadian farmer gets and what the Danish farmer gets in relation to the profits made by the packer. Our packers seem to take all the profits, leaving a small margin of loss for the farmer.
There is another matter to which I would call attention, something I have been working at for the last eight or nine years. I started nine years ago and made a poor success. At one time I was in touch with certain Danish professors; in fact, these gentlemen from Copenhagen were at my home. They said I would never get good bacon and hams from Yorkshire hogs. I had two hundred of them, and these gentlemen laughed at me and said, "These hogs have no hams on them; they have just two posts for hind legs and you will never get hams from them." I got reports from Denmark, and this professor gave me the differentiation between the shoulder and the side. Danish hogs have a larger ham than shoulder. Our Yorkshire hogs are wild animals; they have not been really domesticated. The Danes have beaten us in bacon, eggs, and butter on the British market. Their industry is highly specialized, and I suggest we take advantage of specialization along these lines.
Eight years ago I appealed strongly to the Minister of Agriculture of that day (Mr. Motherwell). One of his assistants was named Arkell, and they wrote to me that they had tried Canadian bacon on the British market and that it tasted better than any Danish bacon. Well, I do not care what they like or do not like. If they want Canadian bacon, we can keep a few Canadian hogs for them; but what we want to know is what the British market wants. You bring them in and leave them here, and surely by that time if they have any disease we shall know." But he said no; for the welfare of the animal husbandry branch he would not.
I am indebted to Hon. Mr. Weir for bringing in these Swedish pigs. I believe he was conscientious and made a noble effort to help the Canadian farmer. Here is the first report on those pigs, and I have followed them carefully since they came in for experiment. I want to draw attention to how these six York pigs compared with the two Landrace pigs. The average age of the York pigs was 189j days, and the average weight was 208 pounds. The average age of the Landrace pigs was 161 days, and the average weight 212 pounds. The Landrace pigs, in 28| days less time, were four pounds heavier than the Yorks. That is the poorest report we have of the Landrace pigs.
The next experiment took place in Hull; I followed them to Hull. These men have told the truth as far as I know, although they were opposed to the pigs. Here we have six Yorks and two Landrace. The Land-race, 55 days younger than some of the Yorks, weigh as much as the Yorks. Hon. members who are not farmers surely can appreciate this: You have two pens of pigs, Yorks and Landrace; you have finished feeding the Landrace pigs and 55 days after they have been shipped, you are still feeding a bunch of Yorks. What is more, I saw a professor there lecture to two hundred farmers and tell them to raise the Yorkshire pig, one of which took fifty-five days longer to grow and dressed four pounds less than the Landrace. I was very angry at the professor: I asked him, "Have you no consideration for the farmer or are you simply considering the grading of pigs for Canada Packers?" He said, "Yes, the time required in growing these pigs should be taken into consideration."

There is just one other point I want to mention. I would like hon. members to notice the age and weight and grade of the Landrace pigs as compared with the Yorkshires. The farmer has to feed a Yorkshire pig for thirty days longer in order to get a lower dressed weight. I could have made it much more than thirty days, but if I am lying I want to be lying on the right side. This partly explains why the Danes are able to buy our grain and drive us off the British market, as they have been doing for years. Last year we only half filled our quota, because we could not afford to feed our pigs. What with the differentiation mentioned by another hon. member, and the type of pigs we are compelled to grow, we cannot compete with the Danes on the British market. I may be wrong,

but it seems to me a real crime against our farmers that this should be permitted. The Swedish pigs should be distributed among our farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I have been very much interested in the discussion this afternoon, particularly in what has been said by the hon. member for Kootenay East and the hon. member for Wellington North. I am a farmer, and I am interested in seeing that the farmer gets as much as possible for his hogs. Perhaps a conversation I had last fall with a pork packer might interest this committee. That conversation was induced by a market report appearing in the Farmer's Advocate, which was called to my attention by one of my neighbour farmers. Under the heading Hog Prices Drop, the article says:
Last week hog prices tumbled from 35 to 50 cents, closing at 8.50 for bacons off trucks at Toronto.
Then several other quotations are given which I need not read. The significant part of this report follows:
Canadian bacon in the old country held steady with the previous week, which was 7 shillings below the same week a year ago. On the other hand Danish bacon was quoted for the week ending September 18 at 15 shillings above the same week a year ago. English, Irish and Swedish bacon were all quoted, the week above mentioned, from 8 to 10 shillings above Canadian.
I wrote the editor of the magazine and asked if that statement was correct, and the reply I received was that he had no reason to think it was not correct. So I went to a pork packing plant not far from' where I live to inquire into the matter, and in the course of our conversation I referred to the price spreads committee, to which the hon. member for Kootenay East referred. Mind you, I hold no brief for the pork packers, but there may be some merit in his reply, which was: "There was something about the production of bacon that the price spreads committee did not get at. He explained it in this way: "We will never have bacon in Canada as uniform in quality as they have in Denmark, because they impart all their feed, and they feed to a formula in order to produce pork of the best quality as cheaply as possible. The quality of pork or bacon that we get in Canada depends largely on the grain grown in the locality where the hogs are fed."
I think there is something in that argument, because as long ago as I can remember I heard farmers discussing the relative qualities of bacon from hogs fed on com and hogs fed on peas. It may be that there is something in the quality of Danish bacon
which cannot be seen or told by the weight of the bacon in the particular grade. I think that is something the Department of Agriculture should take up: Perhaps I should have mentioned these points when the estimates of that department were under consideration, but when the discussion turned this way I thought it would not be improper to introduce this question.
There is just one matter about which I should like to ask the hon. member for Wellington North. Was any record kept of the amount that was fed the Yorkshire pigs and the Landrace pigs?
Records were kept, but I have not an accurate record here. It is in terms which I do not very well understand.

Article agreed to.
On article 6:
The government of Canada undertake that the goods the growth, produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom enumerated in Schedule IV appended hereto, when conveyed without transhipment from any part of the British Empire enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff into a sea, lake or river port of Canada, shall not be subjected to duties of customs higher than those specified in that schedule.
The government of Canada undertake as regards goods the growth, produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom other than those enumerated in Schedule IV that, under the British preferential tariff, no new protective duty shall be imposed and no existing protective duty increased except after an inquiry at which United Kingdom producers shall enjoy full rights of audience.

I should like to say some' thing wth regard to article 6 of the budget What the industrial worker in Canada wants more than anything else is permanency and stability in his job. I quite realize that some of the items contained in schedule IV do not reduce the rates of duty to any great extent, though of course others do. Perhaps the effect on industry just now will not be anything like as detrimental as might have been the case but for the fact that, as everyone knows, every pound of steel that possibly can be imported into Great Britain is being secured by that country, and their shipments of steel are not very great. On the whole the steel industry, on account of the war scare in Europe, is not affected as adversely as it would have been. But what everybody in industry is frightened to death over is this: How far is it going to go? Every year for the last ten years or more of Liberal rule the whole industrial fabric, including hundreds, thousands, and up to a million workers in industry have been alarmed by the constant,

There is a thought ivhich does not receive as much consideration as I think sometimes it should be given in public discussions, and that is the desirability of something like tariff stability. Business men do not like to be always threatened with changes in the tariff. There is no finality in legislation either as respects that tariff or as respects anything else.
Further on he says:
Speaking broadly, it is possible to give the country a reasonable assurance of stability of tariff.
I say the very same thing about the workers in industry. I know something about industry, and about the attitude of mind of the worker. He is just as much interested in tariff schedules as any industrialist, because he knows his job depends on the tariff protecting the plant in which he works. How can there be any permanency in employment if we are going to have anything but permanency in tariff schedules?
Here we have a new set of tariff schedules. The government of the province of Ontario has adopted or is about to adopt a minimum wage regulation. How can they carry out any minimum wage regulation in that province if there is a constantly changing tariff? I submit it would be very difficult to do. When in

office in 1924, the Liberal party cut the tariff on a long list of items. I shall not enumerate them, but will content myself with saying that the list was long, and the change seriously interfered with employment in industry.
No.

I can prove it right now. That is my opinion.

I will give them; I did not intend to do so, but I will. In September, 1924, J. R. Shaw of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, appearing before the unemployment conference in Ottawa told the government of the day that their tariff policy was ruinous to employment in industry, and backed up his statement with a long list of industries which had closed from 1921 to 1924. Among those industries there were 240 making foodstuffs of one kind and another, which in the previous three years had closed their doors as a result of the tariffs imposed by the dominion government. There were 24 tobacco industries; 19 fertilizer industries; 85 connected with oils, chemicals and drugs; 43 making pulp and paper supplies of one kind or another; 271 engaged in the preparation of lumber and wood products; 49 furniture manufacturers-and quite a number of furniture factories are ready to close their doors today; 81 engaged in making building materials, and all kinds of materials in connection with the building industry; 31 concerns manufacturing agricultural implements and tools-

The Minister of Finance is a former premier, as is the Minister of Agriculture. Parliament has done little else in the last year or two but vote for the province of Saskatchewan. Will the hon. member permit a question? He has told us about the industries which closed up. Would he now give us the total number employed in industry between the years 1921 and 1930?

No, but I will do better than that for the hon. member. In a few minutes I shall make a statement in reply to something said a day or two ago by the Postmaster General, because I must set him right. At the same time I will set the hon. member right. The statement was with reference to emigration, and men being thrown out of work.
Give us the number employed.

I would like to proceed in chronological order. May I repeat that in 1922 there were cuts on some 50 odd items. In 1923 there was a ten per cent cut, or a ten per cent discount. In 1924 there was a long list of tariff cuts on all kinds of manufactured goods made by Canadian workers. In 1925 also there was a short but very important list of items cut. In 1926 there were 40 important items cut, but by 1927 the wise words of the late Hon. Mr. Fielding, as uttered in 1923, had apparently sunk in. The castigation and severe thrashing which the government received in the 1925 election for its tariff cuts apparently had sunk in, with the result that in 1927 there were no tariff cuts. In 1928 there were 169 reductions in the tariff, affecting commodities most of which were made by Canadian workers. In 1929 changes were made in 35 items. When the present Minister of Finance came into office in 1930, changes were made in from 250 to 300 items. In the 1936 budget, 150 items more or less were affected, while in connection with this agreement there are 27 pages of items. As one who has been long
associated with industry I say it is about time the Canadian workers and the Canadian manufacturer were given a little relief from attack by the government through the cutting down of tariffs and the cutting out of jobs.
Perhaps I have not gone through the items as closely as I should have, but I have noted some of the changes. The agricultural implement manufacturers are not the bandits and robbers they have been called in this house. In any event, their workmen are as fine as can be found in the world. Those workmen use Canadian products. I am opposed to any interference with the jobs of Canadian workers. What do we find? We find that in 1922, 1923, 1924, 1925, 1926, 1928, 1929 and 1930 there was an attack, either small or large upon the agricultural implement manufacture' and his employees.
In the number employed?
If the hon. member will look at the Canada Year Book he will get the figures of employment in the agricultural implement plants.
There have been very few employed in the manufacture of implements since 1930.

The hon. member knows that a world depression has existed, but even during that time the manufacturers kept quite a number of men employed. In connection with the manufacture of blankets, cottons, flannels, woollens and knitted goods changes were made in 1922, 1923, 1927 and 1928. The same thing has happened in connection with the manufacture of boots and shoes. The tariff on these articles was cut in 1922, 1923, 1928 and, while I am not sure, I believe it is being cut again this year. There are a lot of plants in this country making machinery of one kind or another. I find that the government now in power has always taken delight in crucifying the worker in the machinery plants of this country. Reductions in the machinery tariff were made in 1924, 1925, 1926, 1928, 1929 and 1930. I am not referring to the manufacturers of agricultural machinery; I am referring to the manufacturers of woodworking machinery, iron working machinery, mining machinery and other types.

The hon. member for Davenport has had nearly forty minutes in which to discuss this question, and I crave your attention, Mr. Chairman, for less than ten minutes. My hon. friend suggested that I was not interested in labour. Let me suggest that 'he reconsider this question and face it honestly, as we ought to face it. I am interested in labour; I accept his word that he is interested in labour; I believe that every man in this house-I include also the women- is interested in the employment of Canadian labour at the highest possible wages that can be obtained. But we differ as to the method which will bring about the desired result. My hon. friend thinks a doctrine of exclusion is the proper one; he thinks we must retire from the main street and do business on a back road. I think we should do business in the markets of the world. That is the distinction between Liberalism, on the one hand, and Conservatism on the other. The Conservative looks forward to a contracting world, but the Liberal looks forward to an expanding world. I stand for the expanding world, and my hon. friend stands for a contracting world.
Permit me to prove my assertion, andi as an example I take the city of Hamilton. I take Hamilton because it is a great, proud industrial city, which has made great progress. It is a splendid city. I have been there once or twice, and I like it much better than Toronto because occasionally it returns a Liberal member to this house. In 1922, at the very time when, fate struck the Dominion of Canada, when, a Liberal government was coming into power and when every man in Hamilton ought to have shivered for fear of losing his job, there were 23,475 industrial employees in that city. In 1930, after eight years of that policy, just before the Liberals retired, there were 31,033 workers. I ask my hon. friend to check my figures. He will have time to do that and come back to this chamber before this debate is ended, and he can refute my contentions if I am wrong. Let me go over the figures again. In 1922 there were 23,475 workers; in 1930 there were 31,033 workers. Then lightning struck this country, with a change of government; a gentleman came into power who was going to wipe out all unemployment. We were going to have factories on every corner and prosperity such as men never knew before. In 1934, however, the number of industrial employees in the city of Hamilton had dropped to 24,072, a decrease of nearly 7,000. We were back almost to the level of 1922,-twelve years lost. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about the reductions?

The amount of reductions between this agreement and the old one is not very great. Those reductions are extremely small. I think it goes without saying that they will not be contested too strongly by those who were here in 1932 and listened to the hostile criticism which the agreement introduced in that year received. They will not go so far as to say that they will not have anything to do with this agreement. I voted against the agreement in 1932 and I am not very anxious to support it in 1937, for the reasons I gave earlier in the year. When I see what the Liberal party objected to in 1932 and what they endorsed a few years later, I cannot take their arguments too seriously.
This afternoon and this evening the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) spoke at length and attempted to point out that

Canada-United Kingdom Trade Agreement
tariffs were a great protection for workers in Canada. From the day I came to the house I have maintained that tariffs are practically no protection for the workers. It cannot be shown where they have been a protection by way of keeping their jobs, nor can it be shown that through tariffs the workers have been protected with respect to the wages they have received.
I remember well that at the short session of 1930 tariffs were increased to a great extent. The tariffs on textiles went up; I believe the tariffs on furniture were increased, as were those on many other items. Yet it was not more than a year or so later that the employees engaged in these industries were subjected to reductions in their pay. Not only that, but in spite of the fact that the industries had received increased protection, the workers were unable to retain the jobs they had held in 1929 and 1930.
For these reasons I say that no great amount of importance can be attached to the question of whether a tariff goes up a little or down a little. Sometimes I am amazed at the amount of discussion engaged in by hon. members on the question whether the tariff should go up or down a few points. Of course, I realize that tariffs may be good talking points at election times. I remember what happened at the by-election in Hamilton in 1931, and I would not be afraid to repeat in 1937 exactly what I told the workers in Hamilton in the earlier year when I visited that city during the course of the by-election. I told them then that protection does not protect them at all. The hon. member for Davenport is in his seat, and I will tell him it neither protected them in their jobs nor in their wages, because had it done so there would have been no need for trade unions. If protection worked as some hon. members believe it does, when a tariff is put up wages should go up; but we have had the very reverse. When tariffs went up, wages went down. When tariffs went up in the textile industry, even the volume of employment went down. Volume in industry in the last two or three years has increased when tariffs were high, up to the year 1935, and will probably increase still more after 1935 simply because world volume of trade is increasing. The world volume is of far greater importance to Canada than the question of whether a tariff goes up or down a little bit.

I have seen goods on store shelves that came from other countries and I asked why English goods were not being sold when there was a preference. I found, unfortunately or fortunately as you may want to put it, that the price at which English goods were being offered was the price at which other goods were being offered, with a slight reduction in some cases.
That is not the general principle upon which we have operated with respect to our preference in the English market. I have suggested to the manufacturers in Great Britain that if they expect to seek a market here, they must expect competition. The preference was not meant to inure wholly to their benefit; part of it should be passed on to the consumer, and the consumer would then buy more of their goods. I think that on analysis the minister will find that that is a very mild statement of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In general terms, I would say that all that we heard in the budget debate as to the harm that was to be done to Canadian industry through this agreement cannot be so, if what the leader of the opposition now says is the fact. I submit that neither he nor I can correctly present a matter of this sort in general terms. I think he will agree with me when I say that the test of the situation to which he refers is to be found in a discussion of the individual items under review. I am quite sure that before we get through this schedule the leader of the opposition will be the first to point out the tremendous seriousness of some of the small cuts to which he has now made reference. I would point out that from the consumers' standpoint there is already evidence of benlefit in connection with certain items. I qualify that, as I must, in the light of the general situation to-day in Great Britain, where we have a generally rising price level and a general rise in the cost of production. There has been an even more pronounced rise in the price level in the republic to the south than has occurred in either Great Britain or Canada. Canada seems to be lagging behind somewhat in the general increase in the price level which has become, with one or two notable exceptions, almost world, wide. Because of that fact I submit that no government could adopt the attitude which the hon. member for Davenport recommended we should adopt with respect to tariff matters
The world is not stationary with regard to matters of trade, or with regard to matters of exchange, which is important; matters of trade restrictions, quotas, quantitative regulations and so forth. I do believe that if one could generalize correctly he would say that the tendency throughout the world is more toward the development of international trade thani it is toward the restricting of trade, as was the case during the major portion of the last five years. However, that general tendency needs to be qualified by a detailed study of the effect upon the major items of international trade. What one might say with respect to steel, for instance, would not be equally true with respect to textiles. What one might say with respect to textiles, might not be true with respect to some other major classification in the tariff. What is required, and what this government intends

Canada-United, Kingdom Trade Agreement
to continue to give with the machinery nt its disposal, is a continuous study of the world trade situation, and the empire trade situation. We shall continue to do what we consider is in the best interests of the Canadian people as a whole. If we can, we want to take account of the best interests of all Canadians. I would be the first to admit that every Canadian government is actuated by the same desire.
As I said in introducing the budget, the difference between us are differences as to the method of the attainment of objectives which we all have at heart, and which we can debate as much as we wish. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) takes a somewhat superior attitude with respect to both of the old parties in connection with this question; he says it does not really matter to the worker. Well, there is plenty of evidence that the terms upon which international trade are carried on do matter in many countries,-matter profoundly to the worker. Those of us who are responsible for government cannot adopt the detached attitude of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, and if he occupied a seat in the government I am quite sure that his air of detachment would speedily leave him and he would be quite as conscious as we are of our responsibilities and of the necessity of continuously studying the major factors of international trade.
Now, Mr. Chairman, If I could give a little information regarding extracts of meat, and get on with the job-the proposal is to reduce the tariff against Great Britain with respect to extracts of meat and fluid beef, not medicated, from the present rate of 15 per cent to 10 per cent. Our total imports of these articles in 1936 were valued at $229,000, of which $208,000 came from the United Kingdom. The concession is confined to that portion of the present item 8 of which the United Kingdom is the principal source of supply. As to the balance of tariff item 8 which includes among other things, canned meat, poultry and game, our principal sources of supply apart from our own country are Uruguay and the Argentine. An extract is being made from the item of the tariff of the article in which the United Kingdom is particularly interested, and a reduction of five per cent is proposed in connection with it.

Edwards), I was led by the expressions of fear and the wails of woe that came from that quarter of the house to examine certain figures, which I proposed to put on Hansard
I should like to deal with a point which arose a few moments ago when the leader of the opposition spoke of what he called the inconsistency of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). When we hear of the condition of the workers in our factories, the unemployment they have suffered, and the losses the manufacturers themselves have sustained, may I remind hon. gentlemen that the answer is that the income from their consumers has dropped to about 35 per cent of what it was prior to 1930. The other day the hon. member for Waterloo South spoke of hundreds of men and women having been given employment in Kitchener because of the policies of the present leader of the opposition when he was in office. I would remind him that during the first three years the Conservative administration was in power, namely from 1931 to 1933, unemployment increased in Canada at the rate of about 200,000 a year. So that if the policies of the government of that day did increase employment in Hamilton or Kitchener or some other industrial centre, for each additional man or woman so employed at least six or seven must have been thrown out of work in some other part of the country. My hon. friend has the figures of exports and imports, also whether they are produced in Canada or are entirely imported; that is whether it is a revenue item or a protective item. I would suggest that information should be provided to the committee as a whole in printed form; that is, we should know in regard to each of these items whether it is a revenue item, that is one not produced in Canada but imported, the tariff on it therefore being a revenue tax, or whether it is made in Canada and therefore subject to protection. The minister will see clearly what I am coming at. If an industry carries a wage cost of 25 per cent, and we should happen to discover by examination that it carries a duty rate of 50 per cent, I think it would be admitted that that industry is on relief; that is, the amount of protection we are giving it is more than the wages paid. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

uniformity in presentation, something which for many years past has been badly needed. In fact there is room for very considerable further development along that line, in order that international statistics may be truly comparable with each other. They are not today.
Tor instance, you will find if you look at the records of Swiss imports that Switzerland imports Canadian wheat; but if you look at the records of Canadian exports you would be led to believe that we do not export wheat to Switzerland. No, I must take the opportunity to correct that. My remark to the leader of the opposition was with respect to what we said to the British concerning trade with Canada. I may tell the right hon. gentleman that I said it to the Britishers even before I became a member of the federal government, and I believe my right hon. friend will do me the justice of admitting that fact. I was endeavouring to interest the British in a certain commodity which I hoped to see produced in larger volume in Saskatchewan, and that was one of the answers I had to make. I may tell my right hon. friend that I used then what I used this year as an illustration, namely, the farm implement industry in Canada, and the manner in which it had grown up, and the manner in which the British had lost what market they formerly had through failing to adapt their product to the necessities of a new country and a different system of agriculture. I do not think I was any less vigorous than my right hon. friend in pointing out to the British traders this summer at least some reasons why they do not enjoy more of the Canadian market. I would not accept in all cases the formula he lays down with respect to the British seller always taking advantage to the last degree of the amount of preference granted by our tariff. I admit that in all too many cases that has been true, but in going through the various items with which one had to deal I was surprised to find very many cases in which it was not true. quite see eye to eye with their leader on this matter-
Of course they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-a position opposite to that stressed this evening by the leader of the opposition. I am quite sure the hon. member for Davenport is only waiting to point out instances where the British industrialist is a keen and destructive competitor of the Canadian industrialist. I am quite sure that will be his argument in connection with some of the major fe'atures of the agreement now before the house. We had only to listen to him this afternoon to notice that he was holding a strong rein upon himself until the proper item was reached to pour out the vials of his wrath upon the poor Minister of Finance, who is proposing something which it must be admitted benefits someone in Canada.
Generally speaking, the use of the term "bargaining" is somewhat of a misnomer when used in connection with the negotiation of an agreement of this kind. Obviously, it is ridiculous to say, "I will trade you a concession on boots and shoes if you will trade me a concession on textiles, on wheat or butter or something else," because you are not dealing with comparable articles. When we went horse trading in the old-fashioned sense, we traded one horse for another, or possibly a yoke of oxen or a mule for a horse, but there was always the suggestion of the common utilization of the objects being traded. In negotiating a trade agreement the approach is quite different. I cannot speak for my right hon. friend in this regard, but our approach was to find out what the other fellow wanted, having a very clear idea of what we wanted ourselves. The things were not related nor could the matter be approached in the spirit of horse trading. An effort is made to meet the other man's point of view, without injuring the interests of your own country, to a degree which will encourage him to go as far as possible in connection with what you want. It is a very complex kind of negotiation. So far as the remarks of my right hon. friend with regard to the approach aspect are concerned, let me say that the British are the shrewdest traders I know anything about, and are most dangerous when they are depreciating their own ability along that line.
